extracted.intended_audience: novelists, literary critics, and informed readers (Victorian fiction context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for writing (and judging) novels—especially avoiding clichés and implausibilities in characterization, dialogue, social observation, and use of language. Focuses on verisimilitude, class-knowledge, and preserving the 'life' of language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve historical/living qualities of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid simplifying language into a merely scientific instrument; do not sacrifice the 'music and its passions, and its vital qualities as an expression of individual character' by over-simplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns against a drive to 'simplification' that would leave us with a sterile 'language of the future' (satirically compared to a talking watch). Keep historical texture, wit, humor, and imaginative power in prose rather than reducing language to mechanical precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground depictions in particular, observed social detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A wise treatment of social life should be based on study of the 'natural history of the people'—the special, local, and concrete facts of social groups—rather than abstract, universal theorizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Riehl's method is praised: pause from theorizing and examine what material is actually present. For writers, this implies carefully observing the peculiar characteristics of the nation/province/class you portray rather than relying on broad generalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing a universal social theory on disparate contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not apply one social theory indiscriminately to societies whose conditions differ (e.g., German vs. French vs. English).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticizes Socialists who substitute study of a single fragment (like factory operatives) for an explanation of 'the people' as a whole. For fiction, avoid flattening different social environments into the same template—attend to local differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stock, stereotyped heroines (mind-and-millinery tropes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on the recurrent 'heiress/peeress' heroine who combines implausible perfection: dazzling wit, perfect morals, superb contralto, omnilingual learning, inexhaustible eloquence, and a wardrobe that marks her as exalted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay enumerates the clichés of the 'mind-and-millinery' species (heiress, vicious baronet, amiable duke, irresistible younger son, endless admirers). Such recurrent formulaic composition undermines verisimilitude and reduces interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give supporting characters independent, believable roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce male or other supporting characters to mere ornaments whose only function is to accompany or admire the heroine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic notes that in these novels 'the men play a very subordinate part'; realistic fiction should show that others have working-day business, independent motives, and functions beyond making the heroine shine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in social-class knowledge and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should know and accurately portray different classes instead of treating working classes merely as 'dependents' or misunderstanding basic living conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay condemns novelists who write from boudoirs and have 'no notion of the working-classes except as "dependents"', or who imagine £500 a year to be a 'miserable pittance.' Good fiction requires genuine acquaintance with the lives portrayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-appropriate, believable dialogue and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters—especially children—must speak and act in ways appropriate to their age and experience; avoid giving a four-year-old Ossianic rhapsodies or unrealistic poetic eloquence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: a purported child of four-and-a-half speaks in grand, metaphoric, adult fashion. Such miscasting is an anti-pattern that breaks reader trust and undermines realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility of skills and accomplishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attribute improbable erudition or facility (polyglottism, classical scholarship, instant mastery of Oriental tongues) to characters without plausible grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic ridicules heroines who can read Scriptures 'in their original tongues' and converse in many languages while being otherwise implausible. Skills should be credible within the character's background and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contrived plot devices and convenient resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from using formulaic contrivances—duels that conveniently kill the villain, dying husbands who request their wives to remarry, etc.—as tidy solutions to plot problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay lists common artificial outcomes (villain killed in a duel; tedious husband dies requesting his wife to marry her true love) as symptomatic of poor plotting; such devices cheapen moral and psychological stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist trivialized sentimentality and decorative suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce sorrow and suffering to genteel, ornamental gestures (e.g., 'wept into embroidered pocket-handkerchiefs') that make pain decorous rather than lived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentimentality that sanitizes or decorates suffering is criticized; genuine emotion should feel earned and grounded in real circumstances, not merely ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excess rhetorical exposition and bedroom rhapsodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should not constantly deliver long, elevated speeches or rhapsodies (especially in private moments) that read as authorial exhibition rather than natural expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic observes heroines who 'make speeches, and to rhapsodize at some length when she retires to her bedroom.' Such over-eloquence signals authorial indulgence rather than psychological realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate social conduct and display of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not have characters gratuitously display erudition in socially inappropriate contexts (e.g., quoting Ciceronian Latin at a mixed picnic) unless it's plausible for the character and situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a heroine who quotes Latin in mixed company is judged unrealistic. Display of learning should be integrated plausibly into scene and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not excuse poor craft by imagined authorial privation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the sentimental defense that 'empty writing was excused by an empty stomach' when the actual circumstances show authors are comfortably situated and unversed in other lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay rejects the theory that women wrote silly novels out of destitution; instead it argues many write from comfortable boudoirs. Thus, poor writing should be judged on craft, not excused by assumed hardship.
